The last 15 questions are three passage sets (factual, narrative, literary) of 5 questions each; each set stays together.

questions.question:
Match the phrasal verbs in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Look after
(B) Look into
(C) Look down on
(D) Look forward to

List-II
(I) Investigate
(II) Wait eagerly for
(III) Take care of
(IV) Regard as inferior
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Look after a child — take care of (III); look into a complaint — investigate (I); look down on someone — regard as inferior (IV); look forward to a holiday — wait eagerly for (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps look after and look into; (B) swaps the last two; (C) swaps look into and look down on.
Key point: The particle changes the meaning of "look".

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.sub_topic: Correct sentences: since, furniture, one of those who, did know
questions.question:
Which of the following sentences are grammatically correct?
A. I have been living here since 2019.
B. The furniture in this room are new.
C. He is one of those men who never give up.
D. She did not knew the answer.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: C) A, C and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A and C only
Why: A correctly uses the present perfect continuous with "since". In C, "who" refers to "men", so the plural "give" is right.
Why not the others: B should be "is" ("furniture" is uncountable). D should be "did not know" (after "did", the base form is used). Options (B), (C) and (D) include B or D.
Key point: After do/does/did, use the base form of the verb.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
She studied every evening ________ she could win a scholarship.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) so that
Why: The second clause gives the purpose of studying, so a purpose linker is needed.
Why not the others: (B) and (D) show contrast. (C) shows a condition and makes no sense here.
Key point: "So that" is usually followed by "can/could/will/would".

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in the passive voice:
The police caught the thief near the market.
options: A) The thief is caught by the police near the market.
B) The thief had been caught by the police near the market.
C) The thief was caught by the police near the market.
D) The thief was being caught by the police near the market.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The thief was caught by the police near the market.
Why: The simple past "caught" becomes "was caught" in the passive, and "the thief" becomes the subject.
Why not the others: (A) is in the present. (B) is in the past perfect. (D) is in the past continuous.
Key point: Keep the tense when changing the voice.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
If you do not tie the knot properly, the rope will come ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) loose
Why: "Come loose" means become unfastened; "loose" is the adjective meaning not tight.
Why not the others: (A) "Lose" is a verb meaning to fail to keep. (B) is a noun. (C) "Come lost" is not English.
Key point: Loose (rhymes with goose) is not tight; lose (rhymes with shoes) is to misplace.

questions.sub_topic: Idioms: spill the beans, blue moon, piece of cake, bite the bullet
questions.question:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) To spill the beans
(B) Once in a blue moon
(C) A piece of cake
(D) To bite the bullet

List-II
(I) Very rarely
(II) To reveal a secret
(III) To face something painful with courage
(IV) Something very easy to do
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: Spill the beans — reveal a secret (II); once in a blue moon — very rarely (I); a piece of cake — something very easy (IV); bite the bullet — face something painful bravely (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two; (C) swaps the last two; (D) swaps "once in a blue moon" and "a piece of cake".
Key point: Idioms are learnt as whole units of meaning.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to complete the sentence that begins: "The scientist explained that"
A. because the oceans
B. is melting faster than expected
C. are absorbing more heat
D. the ice in the Arctic
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) D, B, A, C
Why: "The scientist explained that the ice in the Arctic (D) is melting faster than expected (B) because the oceans (A) are absorbing more heat (C)." "Ice" is singular, so it takes "is"; "oceans" is plural, so it takes "are".
Why not the others: (B) gives "the ice ... are absorbing". (C) gives "the oceans is melting". (D) starts the clause with a verb.
Key point: Subject–verb agreement can decide a rearrangement.

questions.question: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to OBSOLETE:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Up-to-date
Why: Obsolete means no longer in use, out of date; its opposite is up-to-date.
Why not the others: (B) and (D) are close in meaning to obsolete. (C) A machine can be obsolete without being broken.
Key point: Typewriters became obsolete when computers spread.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The red scarf is a perfect ________ to her grey coat.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) complement
Why: A "complement" is something that completes or goes well with something else.
Why not the others: (A) "Compliment" means praise. (B) means something added to make up a lack. (D) means a tool.
Key point: Complement completes; compliment praises.

questions.question:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in capitals:
He was RELUCTANT to lend his new bicycle to anyone.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Eager
Why: Reluctant means unwilling and hesitant; eager means keen and wanting to do something.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are synonyms. (D) is related but not opposite.
Key point: Check that the antonym is the same part of speech.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Looking at old photographs of his school, he felt ________ about his childhood.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) nostalgic
Why: "Nostalgic" means feeling a fond longing for the past.
Why not the others: (A) means not caring. (B) means anxious about the future. (C) means jealous of someone else.
Key point: Nostalgia looks back; apprehension looks forward.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The ________ of the college welcomed the new students in the hall.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) principal
Why: "Principal" as a noun means the head of a school or college.
Why not the others: (A) "Principle" means a rule or belief. (C) is an adverb meaning mainly. (D) is an adjective meaning having strong moral rules.
Key point: The principal is your "pal"; a principle is a rule.

questions.sub_topic: Antonym pairs: verbose, humble, vacant, artificial
questions.question:
Select the correct pairs of antonyms:
A. verbose — concise
B. humble — arrogant
C. vacant — empty
D. artificial — natural
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: B) B, C and D only
C) A, B, C and D
D) A, B and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A, B and D only
Why: Verbose (using too many words) and concise, humble and arrogant, artificial and natural are opposites.
Why not the others: Pair C is a pair of synonyms — vacant means empty. Options (A), (B) and (C) include pair C.
Key point: Test each pair on its own before choosing.

questions.question:
Select the words that can describe "a speech given without preparation":
A. extempore
B. verbatim
C. impromptu
D. intrinsic
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: D) A, B and C only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A and C only
Why: "Extempore" and "impromptu" both mean spoken or done without preparation.
Why not the others: B (verbatim) means word for word, as in a speech read exactly from a text. D (intrinsic) means belonging naturally. Options (B), (C) and (D) include one of them.
Key point: An impromptu speech is the opposite of a speech read verbatim.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. planted fifty saplings
B. before the rains began
C. Last Monday, the children
D. along the school wall
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) C, A, D, B
Why: The capitalised opener with the subject (C) comes first, then the verb and object (A), where they were planted (D), and when (B).
Why not the others: (B) puts the place before the verb. (C) starts with a lower-case part. (D) puts the capitalised opener in the middle.
Key point: Subject, verb, object, then place and time.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank:
He felt ________ when he forgot the words of his speech.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) embarrassed
Why: The correct spelling has double "r" and double "s": embarrassed.
Why not the others: (A) has one "r". (B) has one "s". (D) has one "r" and an "e" in place of "a".
Key point: Embarrassed — two Rs and two Ss.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to ELOQUENT:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Articulate
Why: Eloquent means able to speak or write fluently and persuasively; articulate means expressing ideas clearly and well.
Why not the others: (A) means graceful in style or looks. (B) means talking a lot, which is not the same as speaking well. (D) is closer to the opposite.
Key point: An eloquent speaker moves the audience, however few words he uses.

questions.question:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in capitals:
The family moved out of the DILAPIDATED house before the monsoon arrived.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Crumbling
Why: Dilapidated means in a state of ruin because of age or neglect; crumbling means falling to pieces.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) describe a house but not its poor condition.
Key point: The sentence (leaving before the monsoon) hints that the house was unsafe.

questions.question:
Match the figures of speech in List-I with the examples in List-II:

List-I
(A) Simile
(B) Hyperbole
(C) Alliteration
(D) Irony

List-II
(I) I have told you a million times to shut the door.
(II) Silent snakes slid slowly southward.
(III) Her smile was as bright as the morning sun.
(IV) The fire station burnt down last night.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)
Why: "As bright as the morning sun" compares with "as" — simile (III); "a million times" exaggerates — hyperbole (I); repeated "s" sounds — alliteration (II); a fire station destroyed by fire is the opposite of what one expects — irony (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps simile and hyperbole; (C) swaps hyperbole and alliteration; (D) swaps alliteration and irony.
Key point: Irony is a gap between what is expected and what happens.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. that he had left his wallet on the bench
B. did Ravi realise
C. Only when the train
D. had pulled out of the station
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) C, D, B, A
Why: "Only when the train (C) had pulled out of the station (D) did Ravi realise (B) that he had left his wallet on the bench (A)." After an "Only when" clause, the main clause is inverted ("did Ravi realise").
Why not the others: (A) separates "the train" from its verb. (B) puts the "that" clause before "realise". (C) starts with a lower-case part.
Key point: "Only when ..." is followed by inverted word order in the main clause.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct word to fill in the blank:
I prefer tea ________ coffee in the morning.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) to
Why: The pattern is "prefer one thing to another".
Why not the others: (A) "Than" follows comparatives such as "rather" or "better", not "prefer". (B) and (D) are not used with "prefer".
Key point: Prefer X to Y; would rather X than Y.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
After much thought, she made the ________ to study medicine.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) decision
Why: After "made the", a noun is needed: "made the decision".
Why not the others: (A) is a verb. (B) is an adjective. (D) is an adverb.
Key point: An article ("the") is followed by a noun or an adjective + noun.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The business proved so ________ that within two years he had paid off all his loans.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) lucrative
Why: "Lucrative" means producing a lot of money, which explains how he paid off his loans quickly.
Why not the others: (B) means dull and tiring. (C) describes low, unskilled work. (D) means done without payment.
Key point: The result clause ("paid off all his loans") decides the word.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. are expected to rise
B. which have been falling for months,
C. by the end of the year
D. Vegetable prices,
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) D, B, A, C
Why: "Vegetable prices (D), which have been falling for months (B), are expected to rise (A) by the end of the year (C)." The relative clause sits right after the noun it describes.
Why not the others: (A) puts the relative clause after the verb. (C) begins with a lower-case "which". (D) separates the subject from its verb with an unrelated phrase.
Key point: Commas often enclose a "which" clause inside the sentence.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank:
Because of the storm warning, the organisers had to ________ the outdoor concert.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) call off
Why: "Call off" means to cancel.
Why not the others: (A) means to visit or to ask someone formally. (B) means to telephone or to summon for military service. (C) means to demand or require.
Key point: An event is called off; a person is called on.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
________ his injured ankle, he completed the marathon.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Despite
Why: "Despite" is followed by a noun phrase ("his injured ankle") and shows contrast.
Why not the others: (A) "Although" needs a full clause ("Although his ankle was injured"). (C) gives a reason, which is illogical. (D) cannot join a noun phrase to a clause.
Key point: Despite + noun; although + clause.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Within a year, the new student had ________ remarkable progress in English.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) made
Why: The fixed collocation is "make progress".
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) do not go with "progress".
Key point: Make progress, make a decision, make an effort.

questions.question: Choose the one word for: "A person who loves and collects books"
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Bibliophile
Why: A bibliophile (Greek "biblion", book + "philos", loving) is a lover and collector of books.
Why not the others: (A) compiles lists of books. (C) works in a library. (D) collects postage stamps.
Key point: "-phile" means a lover of something.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
Are you interested ________ joining the drama club this year?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) in
Why: The fixed expression is "interested in" something or doing something.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) do not follow "interested".
Key point: Interested in, keen on, good at.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their definitions in List-II:

List-I
(A) Autobiography
(B) Epidemic
(C) Carnivore
(D) Philanthropist

List-II
(I) An animal that eats flesh
(II) The story of a person's life written by that person
(III) A person who gives money and time to help others
(IV) A disease that spreads to many people in an area at the same time
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Autobiography — one's own life story (II); epidemic — a disease spreading widely in an area (IV); carnivore — a flesh-eater (I); philanthropist — one who helps others with money and time (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps epidemic and carnivore; (B) swaps autobiography and philanthropist; (D) swaps carnivore and philanthropist.
Key point: "Auto-" means self; "phil-" means love.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:
A. Then the dough is left to rest for half an hour.
B. To make chapatis, wheat flour is first mixed with water and a pinch of salt.
C. Finally, each round is cooked on a hot tawa until it puffs up.
D. After resting, it is divided into small balls and rolled into thin rounds.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) B, A, D, C
Why: B introduces the process ("first"); A follows with "Then the dough"; D begins "After resting"; C ends with "Finally, each round", which needs the rounds from D.
Why not the others: (A) rolls the dough before it rests. (B) begins with "Then". (D) cooks "each round" before the rounds are made.
Key point: "First", "then", "after" and "finally" mark the order of a process.

questions.question:
Match the sentences in List-I with the prepositions in List-II that fill their blanks:

List-I
(A) She was not aware ____ the change in the timetable.
(B) All members must comply ____ the rules of the club.
(C) This cloth is superior ____ the one we bought last year.
(D) He decided to abstain ____ voting on the proposal.

List-II
(I) to
(II) from
(III) of
(IV) with
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Aware of (III), comply with (IV), superior to (I) and abstain from (II) are fixed combinations.
Why not the others: (A) swaps "with" and "to"; (B) swaps "of" and "with"; (C) swaps "to" and "from".
Key point: "Superior to" and "inferior to" never take "than".

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The rescue team worked ________ through the night to save the trapped miners.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) tirelessly
Why: The blank describes how the team "worked", so an adverb is needed: "worked tirelessly".
Why not the others: (A) is an adjective. (C) means exhausted, the opposite sense. (D) means boring or annoying.
Key point: Verbs are described by adverbs, often ending in -ly.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to AUDACIOUS:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Daring
Why: Audacious means bold and willing to take risks; daring means the same.
Why not the others: (A) means loud enough to be heard and only looks similar. (B) is the opposite. (C) is unrelated.
Key point: Do not choose a word just because it looks like the given word.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in indirect speech:
He said to me, "Where are you going?"
options: A) He asked me where was I going.
B) He told me where I am going.
C) He asked me where I am going.
D) He asked me where I was going.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) He asked me where I was going.
Why: A question is reported with "asked"; the question word order becomes statement order ("where I was going"), "are" becomes "was", and "you" becomes "I".
Why not the others: (A) keeps the question order. (B) uses "told" and keeps the present tense. (C) keeps the present tense.
Key point: In reported questions, the subject comes before the verb.

questions.sub_topic: Share of the Sundarbans in India
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Where the Ganga, the Brahmaputra and the Meghna meet the Bay of Bengal, their waters spread into a maze of channels, mudflats and islands. This is the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world, shared by India and Bangladesh. About forty per cent of it lies in the Indian state of West Bengal.

Mangroves are trees and shrubs that can live in salty water that rises and falls with the tides. Twice a day the sea floods the forest floor and then drains away, leaving soft mud that holds very little oxygen. To survive, many mangroves send up breathing roots, called pneumatophores, which poke out of the mud like rows of pencils and take in air at low tide. Others stand on arching stilt roots that keep them steady in the shifting soil.

The forest is home to a remarkable range of life: fish, crabs, crocodiles, spotted deer, hundreds of kinds of birds and the Royal Bengal tiger, which has learnt to swim between the islands. Its shallow waters are also nurseries where young fish grow before they move out to sea, so the fishing families of the coast depend on them.

The mangroves protect people too. Their dense roots slow down storm waves and hold the soil together, so villages behind a healthy belt of forest usually suffer less when a cyclone strikes. Yet the Sundarbans is under pressure. Rising sea levels, saltier water and the clearing of trees for farms and fish ponds are shrinking parts of the forest. Scientists warn that protecting it is not a luxury but a necessity for the millions who live along this coast.

Question: According to the passage, about how much of the Sundarbans lies in India?
options: D) About a quarter of it
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) About forty per cent
Why: The passage says, "About forty per cent of it lies in the Indian state of West Bengal." The rest is in Bangladesh.
Why not the others: (A) is roughly the share that lies in Bangladesh. (B) and (D) are not stated.
Key point: Detail questions are answered from the exact line.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Where the Ganga, the Brahmaputra and the Meghna meet the Bay of Bengal, their waters spread into a maze of channels, mudflats and islands. Others stand on arching stilt roots that keep them steady in the shifting soil.

Its shallow waters are also nurseries where young fish grow before they move out to sea, so the fishing families of the coast depend on them.

Yet the Sundarbans is under pressure. Rising sea levels, saltier water and the clearing of trees for farms and fish ponds are shrinking parts of the forest. Scientists warn that protecting it is not a luxury but a necessity for the millions who live along this coast.

Question: Why do many mangroves send up breathing roots?
options: A) The tidal mud they grow in holds very little oxygen
B) Their leaves cannot take in any air from the sea breeze
C) The roots help them catch the fish that swim past
D) Tigers and deer cannot climb roots of that kind
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The tidal mud they grow in holds very little oxygen
Why: The tides leave "soft mud that holds very little oxygen. To survive, many mangroves send up breathing roots ... which ... take in air at low tide."
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are not stated anywhere in the passage.
Key point: Look for the cause stated just before "To survive".

questions.sub_topic: Meaning of nurseries in the passage
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Where the Ganga, the Brahmaputra and the Meghna meet the Bay of Bengal, their waters spread into a maze of channels, mudflats and islands. This is the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world, shared by India and Bangladesh. About forty per cent of it lies in the Indian state of West Bengal.

Mangroves are trees and shrubs that can live in salty water that rises and falls with the tides. Twice a day the sea floods the forest floor and then drains away, leaving soft mud that holds very little oxygen. To survive, many mangroves send up breathing roots, called pneumatophores, which poke out of the mud like rows of pencils and take in air at low tide. Others stand on arching stilt roots that keep them steady in the shifting soil.

The forest is home to a remarkable range of life: fish, crabs, crocodiles, spotted deer, hundreds of kinds of birds and the Royal Bengal tiger, which has learnt to swim between the islands. Its shallow waters are also nurseries where young fish grow before they move out to sea, so the fishing families of the coast depend on them.

The mangroves protect people too. Their dense roots slow down storm waves and hold the soil together, so villages behind a healthy belt of forest usually suffer less when a cyclone strikes. Yet the Sundarbans is under pressure. Rising sea levels, saltier water and the clearing of trees for farms and fish ponds are shrinking parts of the forest. Scientists warn that protecting it is not a luxury but a necessity for the millions who live along this coast.

Question: As used in the passage, the "nurseries" of the Sundarbans are:
options: A) Shops where young mangrove plants are sold
B) Schools for the children of fishing families
C) Hospitals for animals hurt in cyclones
D) Sheltered waters where young fish grow up
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Sheltered waters where young fish grow up
Why: The passage says the shallow waters are "nurseries where young fish grow before they move out to sea". The word is used figuratively for a place where the young are raised.
Why not the others: (A) is the everyday meaning of a plant nursery, not the one used here. (B) and (C) are not mentioned.
Key point: A familiar word may carry a figurative meaning in context.

questions.sub_topic: Threat not named for the Sundarbans
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Where the Ganga, the Brahmaputra and the Meghna meet the Bay of Bengal, their waters spread into a maze of channels, mudflats and islands. This is the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world, shared by India and Bangladesh. About forty per cent of it lies in the Indian state of West Bengal.

Mangroves are trees and shrubs that can live in salty water that rises and falls with the tides. Twice a day the sea floods the forest floor and then drains away, leaving soft mud that holds very little oxygen. To survive, many mangroves send up breathing roots, called pneumatophores, which poke out of the mud like rows of pencils and take in air at low tide. Others stand on arching stilt roots that keep them steady in the shifting soil.

The forest is home to a remarkable range of life: fish, crabs, crocodiles, spotted deer, hundreds of kinds of birds and the Royal Bengal tiger, which has learnt to swim between the islands. Its shallow waters are also nurseries where young fish grow before they move out to sea, so the fishing families of the coast depend on them.

The mangroves protect people too. Their dense roots slow down storm waves and hold the soil together, so villages behind a healthy belt of forest usually suffer less when a cyclone strikes. Yet the Sundarbans is under pressure. Rising sea levels, saltier water and the clearing of trees for farms and fish ponds are shrinking parts of the forest. Scientists warn that protecting it is not a luxury but a necessity for the millions who live along this coast.

Question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a threat to the Sundarbans?
options: B) Oil spilt by passing ships
D) Clearing trees for fish ponds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Oil spilt by passing ships
Why: The passage names "rising sea levels, saltier water and the clearing of trees for farms and fish ponds". Oil spills are not mentioned.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are all named in the last paragraph.
Key point: In "NOT mentioned" questions, tick off each option against the passage.

Question: What is the writer's main purpose in the passage?
options: A) To compare the mangroves of India with those of Bangladesh
B) To persuade readers to visit the tigers of West Bengal
C) To describe the Sundarbans and show why it must be protected
D) To explain how cyclones form over the Bay of Bengal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) To describe the Sundarbans and show why it must be protected
Why: The passage describes the forest, its plants and animals and its value, and ends with the warning that protecting it is "a necessity".
Why not the others: (A) No comparison is made. (B) Tourism is not discussed. (D) Cyclones are mentioned only as a danger the forest softens.
Key point: The purpose covers the whole passage, including how it ends.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Every morning on his way to school, Arjun passed the cobbler who sat under the railway bridge. The old man had a tin box of tools, a small iron last and a cracked mirror tied to the pillar behind him. Arjun had never looked at him twice.

Then, one wet July morning, the sole of Arjun's left shoe came loose. It flapped with every step like a hungry mouth, and two boys from his class laughed so loudly that Arjun's ears burnt. He had only ten rupees in his pocket, and the examination began in half an hour.

"Sit," said the cobbler, pointing to a low stool. He took the shoe, turned it over in his rough hands and clicked his tongue. "Cheap glue," he said. "They make shoes to break, so that you buy new ones." Then he set to work, stitching the sole with a thick waxed thread, his needle moving in and out as steadily as a clock.

When he had finished, Arjun held out the ten-rupee note, ashamed that it was so little. The old man pushed his hand away. "Pay me when you pass," he said, and turned to the next customer.

Arjun passed. On the day the results came out, he ran to the bridge with a box of sweets and the money he had saved. The cobbler laughed, took one sweet and refused the money once again. "Bring me your shoes when they are old," he said. "That is payment enough."

Arjun still has those shoes. He outgrew them years ago, but he cannot bring himself to throw them away.

Question: Why was Arjun upset on that July morning?
options: A) He had lost his ten-rupee note on the way
B) His shoe was falling apart just before an examination
C) The cobbler had refused to mend his shoe
D) He had forgotten to study for his examination
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) His shoe was falling apart just before an examination
Why: The sole of his shoe "came loose", his classmates laughed, and "the examination began in half an hour".
Why not the others: (A) He still had the note. (C) The cobbler mended it at once. (D) is not stated.
Key point: Answer from what the passage states.

Question: "Two boys from his class laughed so loudly that Arjun's ears burnt." This means that Arjun:
options: A) Had hurt his ears in the rain
B) Became angry and wanted to fight
C) Could not hear because of the noise
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Felt deeply embarrassed
Why: Burning ears or cheeks are a common way of showing embarrassment; the boys were laughing at his flapping shoe.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) take the phrase literally. (B) Nothing suggests he wanted to fight.
Key point: Read physical descriptions for the feeling they show.

Question: What does the cobbler's remark, "They make shoes to break, so that you buy new ones," suggest about him?
options: A) He wanted Arjun to buy a new pair of shoes
B) He was trying to sell Arjun some better glue
C) He disliked things made carelessly to be thrown away
D) He had once worked in a large shoe factory
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) He disliked things made carelessly to be thrown away
Why: He clicks his tongue at the "cheap glue" and then mends the shoe with strong stitching. He values things made to last.
Why not the others: (A) He repairs the shoe instead. (B) and (D) have no support.
Key point: Inference asks what a remark reveals, not what it literally says.

Question: Why can Arjun not "bring himself to throw away" the old shoes?
options: A) He hopes to wear them again one day
B) They remind him of the cobbler's kindness
C) He has no money to buy a new pair
D) The cobbler has forbidden him to throw them away
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) They remind him of the cobbler's kindness
Why: The shoes carry the memory of the old man who helped him and refused payment; they matter for what they mean, not for their use.
Why not the others: (A) He has outgrown them. (C) and (D) are not stated.
Key point: Endings often turn an object into a symbol.

questions.sub_topic: Figures of speech in the gutters line
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Rain on the Tin Roof

At first a single drop, then two,
like someone tapping, shy and slow,
who is not sure that he may enter —
and then the whole sky lets go.

Now the roof is a drum: a thousand fingers
rattle and hammer, rat-a-tat;
the gutters gurgle, the drainpipe chuckles,
and the cat curls tighter on the mat.

My grandmother sets down her needle
and says the fields will drink tonight;
my father counts the leaks in silence
and moves the buckets left and right.

I lie awake and let it sing me
songs that no radio can play —
of mango boughs and swollen rivers,
of muddy schoolbags, and of May

burning behind us like a fever
we have at last got over. Then,
as softly as it came, it leaves,
and the roof is only tin again.

Question: "The gutters gurgle, the drainpipe chuckles." Which pair of figures of speech is used in this line?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Onomatopoeia and personification
Why: "Gurgle" imitates the sound of running water (onomatopoeia), and a drainpipe that "chuckles" is given a human action (personification).
Why not the others: (A) There is no "like/as" comparison and no irony. (C) No opposites are joined and nothing is called something else. (D) There is no exaggeration and no one is addressed.
Key point: Every part of a paired option must be right.

Question: How do the grandmother and the father react differently to the rain?
options: A) She fears the storm; he enjoys the music of it
B) She complains of the noise; he falls fast asleep
C) She wants it to stop; he hopes it will go on
D) She thinks of the fields; he quietly deals with the leaks

Question: "... and of May / burning behind us like a fever / we have at last got over." These lines suggest that:
options: A) The hot summer has ended, and the rain brings relief
B) The speaker was ill with fever in the month of May
C) A fire broke out in the village during May
D) The rain has made the weather hotter than before
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The hot summer has ended, and the rain brings relief
Why: The heat of May is compared to a fever; the rain is like the moment a fever breaks and the patient recovers.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) read the simile literally. (D) is the opposite.
Key point: Ask what the comparison says about the thing compared.

Question: What does the last line, "and the roof is only tin again," suggest?
options: A) Without the rain, the roof is plain and silent once more
B) The rain has damaged the roof beyond repair
C) The family has decided to replace the whole roof
D) The roof had once been made of a different metal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Without the rain, the roof is plain and silent once more
Why: While it rained, the roof was "a drum" that sang; once the rain leaves, it is just a sheet of tin.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are not suggested anywhere in the poem.
Key point: Closing lines often return to the start with a changed meaning.
